```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = TRUE)
# Bash chunks are a record of commands you ran in the Terminal. Knitting shows
# them but doesn't run them again.
knitr::opts_hooks$set(engine = function(options) {
  if (options$engine == "bash") options$eval <- FALSE
  options
})
```

In this step, I navigated to the flye folder, and then made a link to the black band disease genomic data that I'll be working with.
```{bash}
jd180553@rstudio26:~/bbd-metagenome/flye$ cd ~/bbd-metagenome/flye
ln -s /pvol/data/metagenome_assembly/bbd_0.1.fastq.gz .
```

Then, I created a shell scrip called "run_flye_bbd.sh" with the following code
```{bash}
#!/bin/bash
#SBATCH --time=720
#SBATCH --ntasks=12 --mem=20gb

echo "Starting flye bbd in $(pwd) at $(date)"

flye --nano-hq bbd_0.1.fastq.gz --threads 12 --out-dir bbd --meta

echo "Finished flye bbd in $(pwd) at $(date)"
```

In this step, I submitted the job set up in my shell script.
```{bash}
jd180553@rstudio26:~/bbd-metagenome/flye$ sbatch run_flye_bbd.sh
```

That job took nearly an hour to complete, I know this because I ran the following code, which details the job ID, its state (timeout, out_of_memory, or in this case complete), and how much time elapsed while running the program.
```{bash}
jd180553@rstudio26:~/bbd-metagenome/flye$ sacct -j 447 --format=JobID,State,MaxRSS,Elapsed
```

Assembly of the BBD nanopore reads with Flye. Commands for this step were run in `flye/`.
